sourceInformation.source: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982), directed by Steven Spielberg, written by Melissa Mathison
sourceInformation.genre: Adventure, stealth, environmental puzzle, bicycle flight
sourceInformation.perspective: Third-person three-quarter exploration with a cinematic chase camera during flight
sourceInformation.tech: Three.js r180 (0.180.0), WebGPURenderer with WebGL2 compatibility, Rapier 0.19.3, Gamepad API, Web Audio API, PeerJS 1.5.5, AI Hub Session Protocol v1 client 1.4.0
sourceInformation.artDirection: Procedural stylized cel shading, stepped toon lighting, ink outlines, moonlit pines and warm suburban windows
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js AnimationMixer, AnimationClip and keyframe tracks for walking, pedaling, breathing, alien wonder and fingerlight; procedural bicycle wheels, flight, botanical recovery and departure motion
sourceInformation.audio: Original code-synthesized adaptive music, effects and Animalese-style alien/child gibberish; music defaults to 10%; no audio files
sourceInformation.online: 1–4-player ghost rides through AI Hub Session Protocol v1; standalone PeerJS 1.5.5 WebRTC rooms with same-origin BroadcastChannel fallback. Independent WAN/NAT traversal: unknown.
sourceInformation.testing: Headless fixed-step complete playthrough, Rapier collision and recovery checks, melody-error recovery, emulated standard gamepad, phone multitouch, Offline Web Audio PCM analysis, file:// launch, two-page multiplayer, separate-origin WebRTC probe and unchanged AI Hub automatic harness (2 players; 4 players with 150 ms latency, 50 ms jitter, 5% loss; host departure). Screenshots check composition. Physical controller, real iOS, independent WAN and human listening: unknown.
sourceInformation.research: AFI film synopsis, Amblin film page and Library of Congress film essay; Three.js r180 toon/WebGPU source, Rapier JavaScript documentation, PeerJS documentation and AI Hub protocol/harness

testingFeedback: Testing caught 10 distinct game issues: blocked autopilot waypoints, the first-tap touch HUD, a black compatibility sky, a clipped moon, title character orientation, bicycle riding pose, Hub readiness timing a background-tab room countdown, a balance-reset regression introduced by per-file formatting, and uneven phone-menu margins. All were corrected.

3 were flow breaking in the affected modes: the attract tour could stall, a Hub copy could miss readiness, and a background standalone room could wait for a render frame. No known critical issue remains after the final checks.

The complete fixed-step playthrough using the actual movement, collision, interaction and puzzle systems. It found obstructed routes and proved the transmitter, bicycle, four flight rings, farewell and result screen were reachable in sequence.
The initial headless WebGPU screenshot. It was blank even though the requested backend and physics initialized, so it could not judge the art; WebGL2 screenshots supplied the visual check.
engineFeedback: Three.js r180 provides native toon node materials, TSL and AnimationMixer in the same scene graph. These made procedural ink-edged art and authored character animation practical without external assets.

Yes. An equirectangular canvas background rendered black on the compatibility path; a TSL sky dome fixed it. Announcing a Hub copy before its scene finished loading also exposed the readiness deadline, so connection and readiness now follow loading.

The adventure state machine, camera and interaction rules, controller focus navigation, assisted touch input, and ghost-room transport. Rapier supplies collision and a real lifted crate; the game defines what those events mean.

Validating WebGPU rendering in a headless software environment while keeping the WebGL2 compatibility scene visually consistent. Native walk/pedal animation blending and asynchronous multiplayer startup also needed careful coordination.
none. Engine and physics library code are unmodified. Custom shaders, geometry, animation clips, recovery rules and networking live in the game.
A reliable headless image readback and clearer diagnostics when a WebGPU device or capture produces no useful pixels.
promptFeedback: The source, complete vertical-slice requirement, controller-first UX and executable test expectations gave the adaptation a clear shape. Friendship, homemade communication and the bicycle flight could become connected mechanics.

Mechanics, levels and enemies must be inferred for a film source. The required Hub protocol defines session networking, while the standalone room service and the choice between co-op, ghost and competitive play are left open.
Making the exploration, stealth, musical puzzle, bicycle flight, native animations, synthesized audio and three input styles form one complete journey inside a single shareable HTML file.

Specify the intended multiplayer relationship and the expected standalone signaling or hosting service. For film sources, explicitly describe mechanics and level research as adaptation of scenes and themes.

aiHub.name: E.T. the Extra-Lost-and-Found
aiHub.tagline: A pocketful of candy. A sky full of home.
aiHub.description: Befriend a stranded visitor, sneak through a moonlit neighborhood, and build a telephone out of little things. Then take the bicycle past bedtime and into the stars, alone or alongside up to three ghost riders.
aiHub.controls: WASD / left stick move; mouse drag / right stick look; E / Cross interact; Space / Square glow; Shift / Circle sneak; Q / R1 candy; Shift / R2 pedal harder; hold Space / Cross to rise in flight; Tab / L1 map; Esc / Options pause; assisted touch controls
